title: The Book of Jeremiah Timeline
sub: The Weeping Prophet · A Broken Covenant and a New One Written on the Heart
desc: Forty years of preaching to a nation that would not listen (the temple sermon, the potter's house, a scroll burned column by column, a field bought while Jerusalem burns) build to the promise of a new covenant written on the heart, then to the fall of the city itself and a long sequence of oracles against the nations, Babylon included.

eras.label: Era I · Jeremiah 1
eras.name: The Call of Jeremiah
eras.dates: A priest's son from Anathoth is told he was set apart as a prophet before he was even born, and when he protests he is too young, the LORD touches his mouth and gives him a commission over nations and kingdoms: confirmed by two brief visions of an almond branch and a tipped pot of boiling water pointed ominously toward the north.

events.title: "Before I Formed You in the Womb, I Chose You"
events.detail: Jeremiah's protest that he is too young to speak is overridden by the LORD reaching out to touch his mouth, appointing him with authority "to uproot and tear down, destroy and demolish, rebuild and firmly plant": a commission over nations, not merely his own people.

verses.text: "Before I formed you in your mother's womb, I chose you. Before you were born, I set you apart. I appointed you to be a prophet to the nations."
the LORD [Yahweh] reached out his hand and touched my mouth and said to me, "I will most assuredly give you the words you are to speak for me."

events.title: An Almond Branch and a Boiling Pot
events.detail: Two brief visions confirm the commission: an almond branch (a wordplay on the Hebrew for "watching") shows the LORD is watching to see his threats carried out, and a pot of boiling water tipped from the north previews the exact direction disaster will come from.

verses.text: "I, the LORD [Yahweh], hereby promise to make you as strong as a fortified city, an iron pillar, and a bronze wall. You will be able to stand up against all who live in the land."

eras.label: Era II · Jeremiah 2
eras.name: Israel's Bridal Love Turned to Prostitution
eras.dates: The book's opening extended oracle recalls Israel's devoted early love for the LORD like a new bride, only to accuse her of trading a fountain of living water for cracked cisterns of her own making, chasing foreign gods with the shameless persistence of a wild donkey in heat.

events.title: "They Have Rejected Me, the Fountain of Life-Giving Water"
events.detail: The LORD recalls Israel's early devotion "like a new bride" in the wilderness, before accusing her of a double wrong, rejecting the fountain of living water and digging cracked cisterns of her own that cannot even hold water.

verses.text: "my people have committed a double wrong: They have rejected me, the fountain of life-giving water, and they have dug cisterns for themselves, cracked cisterns that cannot even hold water."

events.title: "A Wild Female Donkey... in Heat"
events.detail: Israel's pursuit of foreign gods is described in the book's most blunt sexual imagery yet, and the chapter notes the absurdity that a nation with "as many gods as you have towns" still turns to the LORD the moment real trouble comes.

verses.text: "they say to a wooden idol, 'You are my father.'… Yet when they are in trouble, they say, 'Come and save us!' But where are the gods you made for yourselves? Let them save you when you are in trouble."

events.title: "I Have Not Done Anything Wrong"
events.detail: The chapter closes on Judah's flat denial of guilt despite clothes stained with the blood of the innocent poor, and a warning that seeking help from Egypt will fail exactly as seeking help from Assyria already did.

eras.label: Era III · Jeremiah 3
eras.name: Two Unfaithful Sisters, Israel and Judah
eras.dates: Using the language of Mosaic divorce law, the LORD describes having formally divorced wayward Israel for her unfaithfulness, yet her sister Judah watched the whole thing and went and did the same, so an offer to "come back" is extended anyway, promising leaders who lead with knowledge and insight instead of stubborn hearts.

events.title: "So What Makes You Think You Can Return to Me?"
events.detail: Citing the law that a divorced woman who remarries can never return to her first husband, the LORD notes Israel's prostitution to many gods should make any return impossible, yet the question itself leaves the door open.

events.title: Israel Divorced, Judah Watched and Did the Same
events.detail: The LORD describes formally divorcing wayward Israel for her adultery with other gods, yet her sister Judah watched the entire spectacle and, rather than learning from it, went and imitated it, making Judah's guilt the more inexcusable of the two.

verses.text: I sent her away and gave her divorce papers. But still her unfaithful sister Judah was not afraid, and she too went and gave herself like a prostitute to other gods.

events.title: "Come Back to Me, Wayward Israel"
events.detail: Despite the divorce, the LORD extends an open invitation north to exiled Israel, promising leaders who will actually lead with knowledge and a day when the ark of the covenant itself will no longer even need to be remembered.

verses.text: "Come back to me, my wayward sons," says the LORD [Yahweh], "for I am your true master… I will give you leaders who will be faithful to me. They will lead you with knowledge and insight."

events.title: A Noisy, Overdue Confession
events.detail: The chapter closes with the people themselves finally acknowledging that their noisy worship on the hills never helped them, confessing shame and disgrace "for we have sinned against the LORD our God, both we and our ancestors."

eras.label: Era IV · Jeremiah 4
eras.name: The Foe From the North, and a Wound That Cannot Heal
eras.dates: An invading army from the north is pictured approaching like a lion from its lair, and Jeremiah's own visceral reaction (writhing anguish, a pounding heart, a vision of the whole created order unraveling back toward formlessness) makes the coming disaster feel less like prediction and more like something he is already living through.

events.title: "Break Up Your Unplowed Ground"
events.detail: A conditional offer of restoration, genuine repentance could still avert disaster, gives way almost immediately to an urgent trumpet call as "the one who destroys nations" sets out from the north.

events.title: A Scorching Wind, Not a Gentle Breeze
events.detail: The coming judgment is pictured as a wind too fierce for winnowing grain, with an enemy approaching "like gathering clouds" and horses swifter than eagles, provoking Jeremiah's own cry that the people are already doomed.

verses.text: Look! The enemy is approaching like gathering clouds. The roar of his chariots is like that of a whirlwind. His horses move more swiftly than eagles.

events.title: "I Looked… and There Were No More People"
events.detail: In one of the book's most visceral passages, Jeremiah's own body reacts to the vision he sees (a writhing heart, a pounding chest) as he watches creation itself unravel back toward the formless emptiness of Genesis 1, though the LORD notes he will not completely destroy it.

verses.text: I looked at the land and saw that it was an empty wasteland. I looked up at the sky, and its light had vanished.
Oh, the feeling in the pit of my stomach! I writhe in anguish. Oh, the pain in my heart! My heart pounds within me.

eras.label: Era V · Jeremiah 5
eras.name: Not a Single Honest Person to Be Found
eras.dates: The LORD sends Jeremiah searching Jerusalem's streets for even one person who deals honestly, from the ignorant poor up through the supposedly wiser leaders, and finds none: a moral failure the chapter attributes to prophets and priests alike growing "fat and sleek" on fraud while somehow still finding it easy to deny that any of it is really happening.

events.title: "See If Any of You Can Find a Single Person Who Deals Honestly"
events.detail: The LORD sends Jeremiah searching Jerusalem's streets and squares for even one truthful, faithful person, offering to spare the whole city if just one is found, and finds instead people "as hardheaded as a rock" from the poorest to the most educated among them.

verses.text: Go up and down through the streets of Jerusalem. Look around and see for yourselves. Search through its public squares. See if any of you can find a single person who deals honestly and tries to be truthful. If you can, then I will not punish this city.

events.title: A Nation Whose Language You Will Not Know
events.detail: A distant, ancient nation with an incomprehensible language is announced as the LORD's chosen instrument of judgment, precisely because the people denied that prophets speaking of war and famine were speaking the truth.

events.title: A Boundary the Sea Can Never Cross
events.detail: The LORD who sets an unbreakable boundary for the sea's waves contrasts it with a people who cross every boundary he sets for them, growing rich and "fat and sleek" on fraud while priests and prophets alike profit from lies the people themselves seem to love.

verses.text: "You should fear me!" says the LORD [Yahweh]. "You should tremble in awe before me! I made the sand to be a boundary for the sea, a permanent barrier that it can never cross."
The prophets prophesy lies. The priests exercise power by their own authority. And my people love to have it this way.

eras.label: Era VI · Jeremiah 6
eras.name: Refined but Rejected — the Bellows Burn in Vain
eras.dates: Jerusalem is pictured under active siege, its leaders offering only the superficial reassurance "everything will be all right" while the LORD, working like a metal assayer testing ore, finds a refining process that has simply failed: the wicked are too much like rejected silver to be purified by any normal fire.

events.title: "Run for Safety, People of Benjamin!"
events.detail: An urgent evacuation warning pictures Jerusalem as a delicate maiden about to be besieged by armies debating whether to attack at noon or under cover of night, condemned as a city where "nothing but oppression happens."

events.title: "Everything Will Be All Right!" But It Is Not
events.detail: Prophets and priests alike are condemned for offering only superficial comfort, "everything will be all right", to people so far gone in shamelessness "they do not even know how to blush."

verses.text: They offer only superficial help for the harm my people have suffered. They say, "Everything will be all right!" But everything is not all right!

events.title: "Ask Where the Old, Reliable Paths Are"
events.detail: The LORD offers a simple, ancient path leading to rest for the soul, and the people's flat refusal, "we will not follow it," becomes the book's recurring shorthand for willful, informed rebellion rather than ignorance.

verses.text: "You are standing at the crossroads. So consider your path. Ask where the old, reliable paths are. Ask where the path is that leads to blessing and follow it. If you do, you will find rest for your souls." But they said, "We will not follow it!"

events.title: Rejected Silver: the Refining Process Has Failed
events.detail: Jeremiah, appointed "like a metal assayer" to test the people as ore, reports back that the refining fire burns uselessly against too much dross: the people have simply been declared "rejected silver" by the LORD himself.

verses.text: The fiery bellows of judgment burn fiercely. But there is too much dross to be removed. The process of refining them has proved useless… They are regarded as 'rejected silver' because the LORD [Yahweh] rejects them.

eras.label: Era VII · Jeremiah 7
eras.name: The Temple Sermon: "Is This Temple a Hideout for Robbers?"
eras.dates: Standing at the temple gate itself, Jeremiah confronts the empty superstition of a people chanting "the temple of the LORD is here!" three times as if the building's mere presence guaranteed their safety, warning that the LORD once let Shiloh's own sanctuary be destroyed and will do the same to this one.

events.title: "The Temple of the LORD Is Here! The Temple of the LORD Is Here!"
events.detail: Standing at the temple gate, Jeremiah confronts a false confidence chanted three times over, that the temple's mere existence guarantees Judah's safety, and warns that the LORD once destroyed his own sanctuary at Shiloh and will do the same here if the people keep treating the temple as "a hideout for robbers."

verses.text: "You steal. You murder. You commit adultery… Then you come and stand in my presence in this temple… and say, 'We are safe!' … Do you think this temple I have claimed as my own is to be a hideout for robbers?"

events.title: "Do Not Pray for These People"
events.detail: The LORD tells Jeremiah outright not to intercede for the nation, describing whole families cooperating to bake cakes for the goddess called the Queen of Heaven: worship the LORD says troubles no one but the worshipers themselves.

verses.text: "do not pray for these people. Do not raise a cry of prayer for them! Do not plead with me to save them, because I will not listen to you."

events.title: Obedience, Not Sacrifice, Was the Original Command
events.detail: The LORD recalls that the exodus generation was never primarily commanded about burnt offerings, but simply to obey: a demand each successive generation has failed progressively worse than the one before it.

events.title: The Valley of Slaughter
events.detail: Child sacrifice practiced at Topheth in the Valley of Ben Hinnom, something the LORD insists "never even entered my mind" to command, earns the valley a new name, the Valley of Slaughter, so filled with the dead that burial space itself will run out.

verses.text: They have also built places of worship in a place called Topheth… so that they can sacrifice their sons and daughters by fire. That is something I never commanded them to do! Indeed, it never even entered my mind to command such a thing!

eras.label: Era VIII · Jeremiah 8
eras.name: "Is There No Balm in Gilead?"
eras.dates: A catalog of willful, unnatural refusal (even migratory birds know when it is time to move, but the people ignore the LORD's clear requirements) builds to one of the book's most quoted lines, an aching question over why healing never seems to come for a people who could easily find it. This chapter's final verse is numbered as the opening of chapter 9 in most English translations.

events.title: Even the Stork Knows Its Season
events.detail: Unburied royal bones exposed to the sun and stars picture the coming disgrace, while the people's willful ignorance is contrasted sharply with migratory birds who instinctively know their proper times: "my people pay no attention to what I, the LORD, require of them."

verses.text: Even the stork knows when it is time to move on. The turtledove, swallow, and crane recognize the normal times for their migration. But my people pay no attention to what I, the LORD [Yahweh], require of them.

events.title: "Is There No Balm in Gilead? Is There No Physician There?"
events.detail: The people's false hope of peace collapses into genuine panic at the sound of approaching horses, and the chapter closes on one of Scripture's most quoted aching questions: a medicinal balm was available in Gilead, so why has healing still not come? (Its final verse is numbered as Jeremiah 9:1 in most English translations.)

verses.text: There is still medicinal ointment available in Gilead! There is still a physician there! Why then have my dear people not been restored to health?

eras.label: Era IX · Jeremiah 9
eras.name: A Fountain of Tears, and True Boasting
eras.dates: Jeremiah wishes his head were a fountain of tears so he could properly mourn his dying people, describing a society so corrupted by lies that no one can trust even close friends and relatives, before the chapter turns to redefine what is actually worth boasting about: not wisdom, power, or riches, but simply knowing the LORD. This chapter is numbered one verse earlier in most English Bibles, since NET's own text marks the underlying Hebrew boundary at what it calls 8:23/9:1.

events.title: "I Wish My Head Were a Well Full of Water"
events.detail: Jeremiah's own grief opens the chapter, wishing for tears enough to properly mourn his people, before describing a society where deceit has become so total that "everyone must be on his guard around his friends," not even trusting close relatives, met with the LORD's own plan to purify them in the fires of affliction. (Numbered 9:1-17 in most English translations.)

verses.text: I wish that my head were a well full of water and my eyes were a fountain full of tears! … Everyone must be on his guard around his friends. He must not even trust any of his relatives.

events.title: "Let the One Who Boasts Boast in This: That He Understands and Knows Me"
events.detail: Professional mourning women are summoned to grieve a devastation so total that death has "climbed in through our windows," before the chapter closes on a redefinition of true boasting, not wisdom, power, or wealth, but understanding and knowing the LORD, who "acts out of faithfulness, fairness, and justice." (Numbered 9:18-26 in most English translations.)

verses.text: "Wise people should not boast that they are wise… If people want to boast, they should boast about this: They should boast that they understand and know me… that I, the LORD [Yahweh], act out of faithfulness, fairness, and justice."

eras.label: Era X · Jeremiah 10
eras.name: Idols That Cannot Talk, and the God Who Made Everything
eras.dates: A satirical portrait of idols as scarecrows that must be carried because they cannot walk gives way to a genuine hymn of praise to the LORD as the one true, living God who made the earth by his own power: a passage nearly repeated word for word later in the book's oracle against Babylon itself.

events.title: Idols Like Scarecrows in a Cucumber Field
events.detail: Idols carved from felled trees and decorated with imported silver and gold are mocked as scarecrows that must be carried because they cannot walk, set against a genuine hymn declaring the LORD alone made the earth by his power, established the world by his wisdom, and spread out the skies by his understanding: language the book repeats almost verbatim in its later oracle against Babylon.

verses.text: Such idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field. They cannot talk. They must be carried because they cannot walk. Do not be afraid of them because they cannot hurt you.
The LORD [Yahweh] is the one who by his power made the earth. He is the one who by his wisdom established the world. And by his understanding, he spread out the skies.

events.title: "Correct Us, LORD, but Only in Due Measure"
events.detail: Facing the reality of coming exile, the chapter closes with Jeremiah's own prayer acknowledging that people cannot control their own destiny, asking specifically for discipline measured in proportion rather than anger that would "reduce us to nothing."

verses.text: "we know that people do not control their own destiny… Correct us, LORD [Yahweh], but only in due measure. Do not punish us in anger, or you will reduce us to nothing."

eras.label: Era XI · Jeremiah 11-12
eras.name: A Broken Covenant, a Conspiracy From Anathoth, and "Why Do the Wicked Prosper?"
eras.dates: The exodus covenant's terms are recited and declared broken, Jeremiah learns his own hometown of Anathoth is plotting to kill him for his preaching, and his resulting complaint: why do treacherous people prosper while he suffers for his faithfulness? It draws a startlingly personal reply from a God who admits his own land is filled with grief over what has been done to it.

events.title: The Covenant's Terms, and Its Violation
events.detail: The exodus covenant's original terms, obedience in exchange for the promised land, are recited and declared broken by "the stubborn inclinations of his own wicked heart," with the LORD noting Judah now has as many gods as it has towns.

events.title: A Conspiracy From Jeremiah's Own Hometown
events.detail: Jeremiah learns that men from his own hometown of Anathoth are plotting to kill him for his preaching, having been "like a docile lamb ready to be led to the slaughter" without even realizing the danger he was in.

verses.text: I had been like a docile lamb ready to be led to the slaughter. I did not know they were making plans to kill me.

events.title: "Why Are Wicked People Successful?"
events.detail: Jeremiah voices one of Scripture's clearest complaints about theodicy: why do dishonest people prosper and put down roots like healthy trees? He receives the unsettling reply that if he is already worn out racing against men on foot, he will not be able to compete against horses.

verses.text: Lord, you have always been fair whenever I have complained to you. However, I would like to speak with you about the disposition of justice. Why are wicked people successful? Why do all dishonest people have such easy lives?

events.title: The LORD's Own Grief Over His Land
events.detail: In an unusually personal turn, the LORD describes abandoning his own beloved people with visible reluctance, comparing their attack on him to a lion roaring in the forest, before promising even hostile foreign nations mercy if they learn to swear by his name instead of Baal's.

verses.text: "I will abandon my nation. I will forsake the people I call my own. I will turn my beloved people over to the power of their enemies."

eras.label: Era XII · Jeremiah 13
eras.name: The Ruined Linen Shorts
eras.dates: In one of the book's stranger sign-acts, Jeremiah buries a new pair of linen shorts in a rocky crevice, retrieves them ruined many days later, and is told this is exactly what will happen to a nation bound as closely to the LORD as those shorts once clung to his own body: followed by a closing image asking whether a leopard can really change its spots.

events.title: Shorts Buried and Ruined
events.detail: Jeremiah buys, wears, buries, and later retrieves a pair of linen shorts now ruined and good for nothing: a living parable for a nation once bound to the LORD as closely as those shorts once clung to his body, now similarly ruined by its own refusal to obey.

verses.text: "just as shorts cling tightly to a person's body, so I bound the whole nation of Israel and the whole nation of Judah tightly to me." I intended for them to be my special people and to bring me fame, honor, and praise. But they would not obey me.

events.title: Every Wine Jar Is Made to Be Filled With Wine
events.detail: A riddle about wine jars filled with stupor extends into a warning to the royal court itself, urging humility "before he turns the light of deliverance you hope for into the darkness and gloom of exile."

events.title: "Can a Leopard Remove Its Spots?"
events.detail: The chapter closes on one of its bluntest images of ingrained sin (as unchangeable, the text suggests, as an Ethiopian's skin color or a leopard's spots) with Jerusalem's coming shame compared explicitly to a disgraced adulteress exposed.

verses.text: Can an Ethiopian change the color of his skin? Can a leopard remove its spots?

eras.label: Era XIII · Jeremiah 14
eras.name: The Drought
eras.dates: A severe drought becomes the occasion for Jeremiah's own passionate intercession, asking the LORD to act for the honor of his own name even though the people's sins speak against them, but the LORD flatly refuses, revealing that prophets promising "lasting peace and prosperity" instead of this crisis were never actually sent by him at all.

events.title: A Land Cracked Dry, Even the Doe Abandons Her Fawn
events.detail: The drought's severity is measured in human and animal desperation alike (cisterns come up empty, even wild donkeys pant for breath on the hilltops) prompting Jeremiah's plea that the LORD not abandon a people who still belong to him "for the honor of your name."

verses.text: Why should you be like someone who is helpless, like a champion who cannot save anyone? You are indeed with us, and we belong to you. Do not abandon us!

events.title: False Prophets Promising "Lasting Peace"
events.detail: The LORD reveals that prophets telling the people they will never suffer war or famine were never sent by him at all: their reassuring message is pure delusion, and both those false prophets and the people who believed them face the very disaster being denied.

verses.text: "Those prophets are prophesying lies while claiming my authority! I did not send them… 'War and starvation will kill those prophets.'"

eras.label: Era XIV · Jeremiah 15
eras.name: "Even If Moses and Samuel Stood Before Me"
eras.dates: In one of the book's starkest statements of judgment's inevitability, the LORD says even Israel's two greatest historic intercessors could not turn back what is coming, before the chapter shifts into Jeremiah's own rawest personal complaint, cursing the day of his birth in everything but words, and receiving a promise that his suffering itself will become the proof of his prophetic authority.

events.title: "Even If Moses and Samuel Stood Before Me"
events.detail: The LORD names Israel's two greatest historical intercessors and declares that not even they could turn back what is now decreed: judgment traced specifically to the sins of King Manasseh, whose legacy the whole nation will now bear.

verses.text: "Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me pleading for these people, I would not feel pity for them! Get them away from me! Tell them to go away!"

events.title: "Will You Let Me Down… Like a Brook That Cannot Be Relied On?"
events.detail: Jeremiah's rawest personal complaint yet accuses the LORD of being as unreliable as a seasonal streambed that runs dry exactly when needed, drawing a firm reply: repent of such despair, and the LORD will make Jeremiah "as strong as a wall" against everyone who attacks him.

verses.text: Why must I continually suffer such painful anguish?… Will you let me down when I need you, like a brook one goes to for water but that cannot be relied on?
"I will make you as strong as a wall to these people, a fortified wall of bronze. They will attack you, but they will not be able to overcome you."

eras.label: Era XV · Jeremiah 16
eras.name: No Marriage, No Mourning, No Feasting
eras.dates: Jeremiah is told never to marry or have children in this doomed land, and forbidden even from attending funerals or celebrations, his own deliberately isolated life becoming a walking sign of a coming devastation so total that ordinary human milestones will simply stop happening, before a closing promise that a future exodus will one day eclipse even the memory of the first.

events.title: A Prophet Forbidden to Marry, Mourn, or Celebrate
events.detail: In one of the book's most personally costly commands, Jeremiah is forbidden to marry, have children, attend funerals, or join celebrations: his own isolated life becoming a living sign that ordinary human milestones are about to disappear from the land entirely.

verses.text: "Do not get married and do not have children here in this land."

events.title: A New Exodus to Eclipse the First
events.detail: Even amid such stark warning, the chapter closes on hope: a day coming when people will swear oaths not by the exodus from Egypt but by an even greater deliverance yet to come, when the LORD gathers his scattered people home again.

verses.text: "A new time will certainly come… 'as surely as the LORD [Yahweh] lives who delivered the people of Israel from the land of the north and from all the other lands where he had banished them.'"

eras.label: Era XVI · Jeremiah 17
eras.name: The Heart Deceitful Above All Things, and the Sabbath Charge
eras.dates: One of Scripture's most quoted diagnoses of human nature (the heart more deceitful than anything else, and incurably so) is paired with the book's clearest single-issue test case for obedience: whether the people will simply stop carrying loads through Jerusalem's gates on the Sabbath, a small, concrete command the LORD ties directly to the city's entire future.

events.title: "The Heart Is More Deceitful Than Anything Else"
events.detail: Judah's sin is described as permanently engraved on their hearts with a diamond point, framed by one of the book's most quoted lines about human nature in general, and contrasted with the tree-like flourishing promised to anyone who actually trusts the LORD.

verses.text: "The human mind is more deceitful than anything else. It is incurably bad. Who can understand it? I, the LORD [Yahweh], probe into people's minds. I examine people's hearts."
"My blessing is on those people who trust in me… They will be like a tree planted near a stream… It has no need to be concerned in a year of drought."

events.title: Jeremiah's Prayer for Vindication
events.detail: Jeremiah appeals directly to the LORD's own throne as his source of refuge, asking that his persecutors, not himself, be the ones disgraced by the disaster they keep mockingly demanding to see happen.

events.title: The Sabbath Charge at the City Gates
events.detail: A remarkably concrete test of obedience is given at Jerusalem's own gates, simply stop carrying loads through them on the Sabbath, with the entire future of the monarchy and the city itself tied to compliance with this single, specific command.

verses.text: "Be very careful if you value your lives! Do not carry any loads in through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day… But observe the Sabbath day as a day set apart to the LORD [Yahweh]."

eras.label: Era XVII · Jeremiah 18
eras.name: The Potter's House
eras.dates: Watching a potter rework a flawed pot into something new gives Jeremiah the book's clearest picture of how national judgment actually works (conditional, responsive, reversible by genuine repentance) right before the people themselves flatly reject the whole premise and plot Jeremiah's death for saying it.

events.title: "Can I Not Deal With You as This Potter Deals With the Clay?"
events.detail: Watching a potter rework a flawed vessel into something new gives Jeremiah the book's clearest statement of divine flexibility (threats of judgment and promises of blessing alike are conditional, reversible by a nation's actual response) though the people flatly reject even the premise: "we will do whatever we want to do!"

verses.text: "O nation of Israel, can I not deal with you as this potter deals with the clay? In my hands, you, O nation of Israel, are just like the clay in this potter's hand."
"We do not care what you say! We will do whatever we want to do! We will continue to behave wickedly and stubbornly!"

events.title: A Plot Against Jeremiah's Life
events.detail: Some of the people conspire to silence Jeremiah entirely, confident other priests and prophets will still be available to advise them, drawing from Jeremiah one of his harshest imprecatory prayers, asking the LORD not to pardon their plotting.

eras.label: Era XVIII · Jeremiah 19-20
eras.name: The Broken Jar, and Pashhur's Persecution
eras.dates: Jeremiah smashes a clay jar in front of Jerusalem's leaders as a sign of the city's coming, irreversible ruin, and the temple's own chief of security responds by having him flogged and locked in stocks: an ordeal that produces the book's darkest personal confession, Jeremiah cursing the very day of his birth.

events.title: A Clay Jar Smashed "Beyond Repair"
events.detail: Jeremiah buys a potter's jar, carries it to the Hinnom Valley with the city's own elders and priests as witnesses, and smashes it publicly: a deliberately irreversible sign that Jerusalem's coming judgment, unlike the earlier potter's-house image, will not this time be reworked into something new.

verses.text: "I will smash this nation and this city as though it were a potter's vessel that is broken beyond repair."

events.title: Flogged and Locked in the Stocks
events.detail: Pashhur, the temple's chief of security, has Jeremiah flogged and confined in the stocks overnight for prophesying: released the next day only to be told by Jeremiah that his own new name is now "Terror Is Everywhere."

events.title: "Cursed Be the Day I Was Born"
events.detail: The book's rawest personal confession follows the persecution: Jeremiah feels coerced into a prophetic calling that brings him nothing but ridicule, describes the message burning inside him like an uncontainable fire, and closes the chapter cursing the very day of his own birth.

verses.text: his message becomes like a fire locked up inside of me, burning in my heart and soul. I grow weary of trying to hold it in; I cannot contain it.
Cursed be the day I was born! May that day not be blessed when my mother gave birth to me.

eras.label: Era XIX · Jeremiah 21
eras.name: Zedekiah's Desperate Question
eras.dates: With Nebuchadnezzar's army already at the gates, King Zedekiah sends officials hoping Jeremiah will report a miraculous rescue like those of the past, instead receiving the blunt news that the LORD himself will fight against Jerusalem, and that survival now depends on surrendering to the very army under siege.

events.title: "I Myself Will Fight Against You"
events.detail: King Zedekiah's officials come hoping for a miracle rescue from the besieging Babylonian army, but Jeremiah's answer inverts the expectation entirely: the LORD himself will fight against Jerusalem, not for it, offering survival only to those who leave the city and surrender.

verses.text: "I will give you a choice between two courses of action. One will result in life; the other will result in death. Those who stay in this city will die… Those who leave the city and surrender to the Babylonians… will escape with their lives."

eras.label: Era XX · Jeremiah 22
eras.name: Kings Confronted: Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Jeconiah
eras.dates: In rapid succession, Jeremiah addresses Judah's last kings by name: Shallum (Jehoahaz), mourned in exile more than the king who died in battle; Jehoiakim, condemned for building his palace on forced, unpaid labor; and Jeconiah, declared effectively childless as far as the throne of David is concerned.

events.title: A General Charge to the Royal House
events.detail: The palace is addressed directly with a simple conditional (do justice and it stands, ignore it and it becomes rubble) grounding the coming judgment in specific royal failures rather than vague national guilt.

events.title: Shallum Exiled, Jehoiakim's Forced Labor
events.detail: The king who died in exile (Shallum, also called Jehoahaz) is mourned more than the one who died at home, while his successor Jehoiakim is condemned specifically for building a lavish cedar palace using countrymen he refused to pay.

verses.text: Sure to be judged is the king who builds his palace using injustice and treats people unfairly… He makes his countrymen work for him for nothing. He does not pay them for their labor.

events.title: No Mourning for Jehoiakim
events.detail: Jehoiakim is denied even the basic dignity of a mourned death, promised instead the indignity of an unburied corpse "dragged off and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem" like a dead donkey.

events.title: Jeconiah Declared Childless Before the Throne
events.detail: King Jeconiah, though he has actual children, is declared "childless" in the specific sense that matters most: none of his line will ever again occupy David's throne, a judgment whose tension the New Testament genealogies later navigate carefully.

verses.text: "Enroll this man in the register as though he were childless… For none of his sons will succeed in occupying the throne of David or ever succeed in ruling over Judah."

eras.label: Era XXI · Jeremiah 23
eras.name: False Shepherds, the Righteous Branch, and Lying Prophets
eras.dates: Judah's failed kings are condemned as shepherds who scattered rather than cared for their flock, answered by the promise of a coming "righteous Branch" of David who will rule with real justice, before the chapter turns its harshest fire on prophets who invent their own dreams and call them the LORD's word.

events.title: "I Will Raise Up for Them a Righteous Branch"
events.detail: Judah's kings are condemned as shepherds who scattered rather than gathered their flock, directly answered by the promise of a coming Davidic "righteous Branch" who will rule with wisdom and justice under a name meaning "The LORD Has Provided Us With Justice."

verses.text: "a righteous branch, a descendant of David. He will rule over them with wisdom and understanding… This is the name he will go by: 'The LORD [Yahweh] has provided us with justice.'"

events.title: Prophets Who Never Stood in the LORD's Inner Circle
events.detail: Jerusalem's prophets are condemned as being just as corrupt as Samaria's Baal-prophets, offering false comfort to people already doing evil, with the LORD pointedly asking which of them has ever actually "stood in the LORD's inner circle" to hear what he really says.

verses.text: "which of them has ever stood in the LORD's [Yahweh's] inner circle so they could see and hear what he has to say?"

events.title: "Is My Message Not Like a Fire, and Like a Hammer?"
events.detail: The LORD distinguishes sharply between a mere dream and his actual word, as different as straw is from grain, comparing his real message to a purging fire and a rock-shattering hammer, unlike the borrowed, plagiarized "dreams" false prophets steal from one another.

verses.text: "My message is like a fire that purges dross. It is like a hammer that breaks a rock in pieces."

events.title: The Wordplay on "Burden"
events.detail: A closing wordplay turns on the double meaning of the Hebrew word for both "oracle" and "burden": anyone who mockingly calls the LORD's message "burdensome" is told they themselves have become the burden about to be cast away.

eras.label: Era XXII · Jeremiah 24
eras.name: Two Baskets of Figs
eras.dates: After King Jeconiah's deportation, the LORD shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs outside the temple (one full of good fruit, one so rotten it cannot be eaten) and identifies the exiles already in Babylon as the good figs destined for restoration, while those who remained behind or fled to Egypt are the bad figs marked for further disaster.

events.title: Good Figs and Bad Figs
events.detail: In a sharp reversal of expectation, the exiles already deported to Babylon are identified as the good figs the LORD will watch over and restore, while those who stayed behind in Jerusalem or fled to Egypt are the bad figs marked for further ruin: exile, not remaining in the land, turns out to be the path toward hope.

verses.text: "The exiles of Judah whom I sent away from here to the land of Babylon are like those good figs. I consider them to be good. I will look after their welfare and will restore them to this land."

eras.label: Era XXIII · Jeremiah 25
eras.name: The Cup of the LORD's Wrath, and Seventy Years
eras.dates: After twenty-three years of preaching that went unheeded, Jeremiah announces Babylon's seventy-year dominance in specific, timed terms, then acts out a vivid sign, forcing nation after nation, ending with Babylon itself, to drink from a literal cup filled with the wine of the LORD's own wrath.

events.title: Seventy Years of Babylonian Rule Announced
events.detail: After twenty-three years of preaching met with silence, Jeremiah delivers one of the book's most concrete predictions: seventy specific years of subjugation to Babylon, after which Babylon itself will be punished in turn for its own excesses.

verses.text: "This whole area will become a desolate wasteland. These nations will be subject to the king of Babylon for 70 years.'… when the seventy years are over, I will punish the king of Babylon and his nation for their sins."

events.title: The Cup of Wrath Passed to Every Nation
events.detail: In a striking sign-act, Jeremiah is told to make every nation he lists (Jerusalem first, then Egypt, Edom, Moab, Tyre, Sidon, and many others) drink from a literal cup filled with the wine of the LORD's wrath, with Babylon itself required to drink last of all.

verses.text: the LORD, the God of Israel, spoke to me in a vision: "Take this cup from my hand. It is filled with the wine of my wrath. Take it and make the nations to whom I send you drink it."

events.title: The LORD Roars Like a Lion From on High
events.detail: The chapter closes with the LORD pictured roaring from heaven like a lion, bringing judgment reaching "to the ends of the earth" and leaving even the nations' shepherds with no way to run or hide.

eras.label: Era XXIV · Jeremiah 26
eras.name: Jeremiah on Trial for His Life
eras.dates: Preaching the temple sermon a second time nearly gets Jeremiah killed on the spot by an enraged crowd of priests and prophets, until Judah's own officials intervene, citing the precedent of Micah's similar prophecy generations earlier under King Hezekiah: a precedent that spares Jeremiah even as another prophet, Uriah, is extradited from Egypt and executed for saying the same thing.

events.title: Arrested for Prophesying the Temple's Destruction
events.detail: Repeating the temple sermon's warning draws an immediate death threat from the priests and prophets who hear it, forcing Jeremiah to defend himself before Judah's officials with nothing but the plain claim that the LORD, not he, is the source of the warning.

verses.text: "The LORD [Yahweh] sent me to prophesy everything you have heard me say against this temple and against this city."

events.title: Acquitted, While Uriah Is Executed for the Same Message
events.detail: Judah's elders cite Micah's nearly identical prophecy under King Hezekiah as precedent for sparing Jeremiah's life, yet the chapter closes noting that another prophet, Uriah, was extradited from Egypt and executed by King Jehoiakim for delivering that exact same warning.

verses.text: "Micah from Moresheth prophesied during the time Hezekiah was king of Judah… Did not the LORD [Yahweh] forgo destroying them as he threatened he would?"

eras.label: Era XXV · Jeremiah 27-28
eras.name: The Yoke of Babylon, and Hananiah's False Prophecy
eras.dates: Jeremiah wears a literal wooden yoke through Jerusalem to dramatize submission to Babylon as the only path to survival, until the prophet Hananiah publicly breaks it off his neck and promises the exile will end within two years: a confident prediction Jeremiah answers not with an argument, but with Hananiah's own death, exactly as foretold, within the year.

events.title: A Wooden Yoke Worn as a Sign
events.detail: Jeremiah wears an actual wooden yoke through Jerusalem's streets, delivering it as a message to neighboring kings as well: submission to Babylon, however unwelcome, is the one path that preserves both life and land, while resistance guarantees only destruction.

verses.text: "Submit to the yoke of servitude to the king of Babylon. Be subject to him and his people. Then you will continue to live."

events.title: Hananiah Breaks the Yoke: and Dies Within the Year
events.detail: The prophet Hananiah publicly breaks Jeremiah's wooden yoke and confidently predicts Babylon's dominance will end within two years, prompting Jeremiah's sober reply that breaking a wooden yoke only replaces it with an iron one: a confrontation resolved not by debate but by Hananiah's own death exactly seven months later, precisely as Jeremiah predicted.

verses.text: "You have indeed broken the wooden yoke. But you have only succeeded in replacing it with an iron one!"
In the seventh month of that very same year the prophet Hananiah died.

eras.label: Era XXVI · Jeremiah 29
eras.name: A Letter to the Exiles: "Plans to Prosper You"
eras.dates: Jeremiah's written letter to the Babylonian exiles delivers surprising, counterintuitive advice (build houses, plant gardens, seek the welfare of the very city that conquered you) grounded in one of the book's most quoted promises of a hope-filled future still to come after seventy specific years.

events.title: "Build Houses and Settle Down": and "Plans to Prosper You"
events.detail: Rather than promising imminent rescue, Jeremiah's letter to the Babylonian exiles tells them to settle in for the long term (building houses, planting gardens, even praying for the prosperity of their captor city) grounded in the book's most quoted promise of a future and a hope still to come.

verses.text: "Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat what they produce… Work to see that the city where I sent you as exiles enjoys peace and prosperity. Pray to the LORD [Yahweh] for it."
"I know what I have planned for you," says the LORD [Yahweh]. "I have plans to prosper you, not to harm you. I have plans to give you a future filled with hope."

events.title: False Prophets Among the Exiles Too
events.detail: Even in exile, false prophets keep offering premature hope, and two of them, Ahab and Zedekiah, are singled out by name for a shocking specific fate: execution by fire at the hand of the very king of Babylon they claimed the exiles need not fear.

events.title: Shemaiah's Rebuke From Exile
events.detail: A third false prophet, Shemaiah, writes from Babylon demanding Jeremiah be imprisoned for his warnings: a letter Jeremiah himself gets to read, and answers with the announcement that Shemaiah's entire family line will be cut off from ever seeing the good things still to come.

eras.label: Era XXVII · Jeremiah 30
eras.name: The Book of Consolation Begins
eras.dates: Jeremiah is instructed to write down everything that follows in a scroll of its own: a deliberate pivot from decades of judgment oracles into sustained promise, opening with the strange image of strong men doubled over in labor pain before turning to genuine, unqualified healing for wounds the chapter had just called "incurable."

events.title: "Write Everything I Am About to Tell You in a Scroll"
events.detail: A deliberate literary pivot begins here, Jeremiah is told to commit the coming oracles to their own dedicated scroll, opening with the strange, vivid image of strong men doubled over like women in labor as "Jacob's time of trouble" arrives, promising some will nonetheless be rescued out of it.

verses.text: Alas, what a terrible time of trouble it is! There has never been any like it. It is a time of trouble for the descendants of Jacob, but some of them will be rescued out of it.

events.title: "I Will Restore You to Health"
events.detail: Wounds the LORD had just called "incurable" are promised genuine healing after all, framed by a repeated refrain about the LORD's anger not turning back "until he has fully carried out his intended purposes": judgment and restoration presented as two stages of one and the same plan.

verses.text: "I will restore you to health. I will heal your wounds. I, the LORD [Yahweh], affirm it! For you have been called an outcast, Zion, whom no one cares for."

eras.label: Era XXVIII · Jeremiah 31
eras.name: The New Covenant, and Rachel Weeping for Her Children
eras.dates: The Book of Consolation's most celebrated chapter moves from Rachel's inconsolable weeping for her exiled children to the promise of a fundamentally new kind of covenant, not written on stone tablets but directly on the heart, quoted more often in the New Testament than almost any other Old Testament passage.

events.title: "I Have Loved You With an Everlasting Love"
events.detail: A joyful vision of homecoming gathers the blind, the lame, and pregnant women alike into a single returning throng, promising dancing, abundant grain and wine, and grief turned so completely to gladness that mourning itself becomes a thing of the past.

verses.text: "I have loved you with an everlasting love. That is why I have continued to be faithful to you."

events.title: Rachel Weeping for Her Children
events.detail: In one of the Old Testament's most emotionally resonant images, the matriarch Rachel is pictured weeping inconsolably in Ramah for children who are simply gone, language Matthew's Gospel later applies to Herod's slaughter of the innocents, answered by a divine promise that her children truly will return.

verses.text: "A sound is heard in Ramah, a sound of crying in bitter grief. It is the sound of Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because her children are gone."
"Stop crying! … Your children will return from the land of the enemy. I, the LORD [Yahweh], affirm it!"

events.title: No More "Sour Grapes": Individual Responsibility
events.detail: A popular proverb blaming children's suffering on their parents' sins is explicitly retired, replaced by a principle of direct individual responsibility: each person will answer for their own sin alone.

verses.text: "people will no longer say, 'The parents have eaten sour grapes, but the children's teeth have grown numb.' Rather, each person will die for his own sins."

events.title: "I Will Make a New Covenant"
events.detail: The chapter's climax and one of the most theologically consequential passages in the whole Old Testament: a coming covenant that will not be written on stone like the Sinai covenant but directly on the human heart, so that knowing the LORD is no longer something taught but something universally shared, "from the least important to the most important."

verses.text: "a time is coming," says the LORD [Yahweh], "when I will make a new covenant with the people of Israel and Judah."

"I will put my law within them and write it on their hearts and minds… For all of them, from the least important to the most important, will know me," says the LORD [Yahweh]. "For I will forgive their sin and will no longer call to mind the wrong they have done."

eras.label: Era XXIX · Jeremiah 32
eras.name: Jeremiah Buys a Field at Anathoth
eras.dates: While literally imprisoned in the palace courtyard as Babylon's army besieges the very city outside, Jeremiah purchases a field back home in Anathoth and has the deed carefully preserved in a clay jar: an act of pure, calculated hope in a future so certain that ordinary property transactions will resume.

events.title: A Field Bought While the City Is Under Siege
events.detail: Confined in the palace courtyard as Babylon's army besieges Jerusalem outside, Jeremiah buys a field from his cousin at Anathoth and has the deed carefully sealed in a clay jar for long-term preservation: a calculated act of hope that ordinary life, including buying land, will one day resume.

verses.text: "'Take these documents, both the sealed copy of the deed of purchase and the unsealed copy. Put them in a clay jar so that they may be preserved for a long time to come.' … 'Houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in this land.'"

events.title: Jeremiah's Prayer: "Nothing Is Too Hard for You"
events.detail: Jeremiah's own prayer processes the tension between the field he just bought in faith and the siege actively unfolding outside, recounting the LORD's historic power over Egypt as grounds for confidence even now.

events.title: "I Will Take Delight in Doing Good to Them"
events.detail: The LORD's extended answer confirms the city will indeed fall for real, specific, named sins, yet closes with an unequivocal promise of regathering, a new covenant of the heart, and the same specific promise that fields will again be bought "with silver, and deeds of purchase signed, sealed, and witnessed," exactly as Jeremiah has just done.

verses.text: "I am the LORD [Yahweh], the God of all humankind. There is, indeed, nothing too difficult for me."

eras.label: Era XXX · Jeremiah 33
eras.name: A Righteous Branch, and an Unbreakable Covenant
eras.dates: Still imprisoned, Jeremiah receives further promises of healing and restoration, expanding the earlier "righteous Branch" prophecy and anchoring David's dynasty and the Levitical priesthood to something as fixed and unbreakable as the daily cycle of day and night itself.

events.title: "Call on Me in Prayer, and I Will Show You Great and Mysterious Things"
events.detail: An invitation to call on the LORD for insight beyond what is currently known leads into renewed promises of healing for the city and restored sounds of ordinary joy (weddings, thank offerings, shepherds counting their flocks) in towns currently lying in ruins.

verses.text: "Call on me in prayer, and I will answer you. I will show you great and mysterious things that you still do not know about."

events.title: A Covenant as Unbreakable as Day and Night
events.detail: The righteous Branch promise from chapter 23 is repeated and expanded, and the LORD ties his covenant with David's line and the Levitical priesthood to the same fixed law that governs day following night, as unbreakable, he says, as that.

verses.text: "I have made a covenant with the day and with the night that they will always come at their proper times. Only if you people could break that covenant could my covenant with my servant David… ever be broken."

eras.label: Era XXXI · Jeremiah 34
eras.name: Freedom Proclaimed, Then Revoked
eras.dates: With Nebuchadnezzar's army already at the gates, Zedekiah leads Jerusalem in a covenant freeing all Hebrew slaves (a genuine, if late, act of obedience to the Mosaic law) only for the people to seize their freed slaves back the moment the immediate danger seemed to ease, a reversal the LORD answers with his own grim wordplay on "freedom."

events.title: Zedekiah's Fate Foretold
events.detail: Even as judgment is confirmed, Zedekiah personally receives a mixed word: he will not die by violence, but will die in peace and be properly mourned, a small mercy embedded within a much larger disaster.

events.title: Slaves Freed, Then Enslaved Again
events.detail: Jerusalem's leaders make a genuine covenant to free all Hebrew slaves as the Mosaic law required, then reverse course and force them back into slavery once Babylon's siege temporarily lifts, provoking the LORD's own bitter wordplay: since they would not grant true freedom, he will grant them "freedom," the freedom to die by war, famine, and disease.

verses.text: "You have not really obeyed me and granted freedom to your neighbor… Therefore, I will grant you freedom, the freedom to die in war, or by starvation, or disease."

eras.label: Era XXXII · Jeremiah 35
eras.name: The Rechabites' Obedience Shames Judah
eras.dates: Jeremiah offers wine to a clan famous for a generations-old vow never to drink it, build houses, or settle down, and their unwavering obedience to a mere human ancestor's command becomes a pointed, humiliating contrast to Judah's repeated refusal to obey the LORD himself.

events.title: "The Descendants of Jonadab Have Carried Out the Orders of Their Ancestor"
events.detail: The Rechabites, bound for generations to their ancestor Jonadab's vow of abstinence and nomadic simplicity, refuse Jeremiah's offered wine without hesitation: an object lesson deliberately staged to shame Judah, since a family has kept a mere human's command for generations while the nation has repeatedly ignored the LORD's own.

verses.text: "the descendants of Jonadab son of Rechab have carried out the orders that their ancestor gave them. But you people have not obeyed me!"
"Jonadab son of Rechab will never lack a male descendant to serve me."

eras.label: Era XXXIII · Jeremiah 36
eras.name: The Scroll Burned, and Rewritten
eras.dates: Jeremiah dictates decades of prophecy to his scribe Baruch on a single scroll, which King Jehoiakim contemptuously cuts apart column by column and burns in his winter firepot as it is read to him, only for Jeremiah to dictate the entire scroll again from memory, this time with even more added to it.

events.title: Baruch Writes Down Decades of Prophecy
events.detail: Jeremiah, barred from entering the temple himself, dictates everything the LORD has told him since Josiah's reign to his scribe Baruch, who writes it all onto a single scroll to be read publicly on a day of fasting.

events.title: King Jehoiakim Burns the Scroll, Column by Column
events.detail: As the scroll is read to him in his winter quarters, King Jehoiakim methodically cuts off each finished section with a knife and feeds it into the firepot in front of him, showing no alarm at all, even ignoring three officials who specifically urged him not to burn it.

verses.text: As soon as Jehudi had read three or four columns of the scroll, the king would cut them off with a penknife and throw them on the fire… Neither he nor any of his attendants showed any alarm when they heard all that had been read.

events.title: Rewritten, With Even More Added
events.detail: Rather than silencing the message, the burned scroll is simply dictated again from memory onto a fresh one, and this time additional prophecies are added to it: the king's destruction of the physical document accomplishing nothing but delay.

verses.text: Jeremiah got another scroll and gave it to the scribe Baruch… As Jeremiah dictated, Baruch wrote on this scroll everything that had been on the scroll that King Jehoiakim of Judah burned in the fire. They also added on this scroll several other messages of the same kind.

eras.label: Era XXXIV · Jeremiah 37
eras.name: Jeremiah Arrested as a Deserter
eras.dates: During a brief lull in the siege when Egypt's army draws the Babylonians away, Jeremiah tries to leave Jerusalem on personal business and is arrested at the city gate on suspicion of desertion: flogged and imprisoned in a private dungeon despite his denial, though King Zedekiah quietly seeks him out anyway for one more private word from the LORD.

events.title: Arrested at the Gate, Interrogated in Private
events.detail: With Babylon's siege temporarily lifted because Egypt's army is approaching, Jeremiah attempts to leave the city on a personal errand and is seized at the gate on a false charge of desertion, flogged, and imprisoned, yet Zedekiah still secretly summons him for one more private, off-the-record message from the LORD.

verses.text: the king questioned him privately and asked him, "Is there any message from the LORD [Yahweh]?" Jeremiah answered, "Yes, there is." Then he announced, "You will be handed over to the king of Babylon."

eras.label: Era XXXV · Jeremiah 38
eras.name: Thrown Into the Cistern, Rescued by Ebed-Melech
eras.dates: Officials furious at Jeremiah's demoralizing message lower him into a muddy cistern to die, until a foreign court official, Ebed-Melech the Ethiopian, intervenes directly with the king to pull him back out, after which a desperate, secretive Zedekiah seeks Jeremiah's counsel one final time, ultimately too afraid of his own officials to act on it.

events.title: Ebed-Melech the Ethiopian Rescues Jeremiah
events.detail: Angry officials lower Jeremiah into an empty cistern where he sinks into the mud to die, until Ebed-Melech, a foreign court official, personally appeals to the king and organizes his rescue with old rags to pad the ropes: an outsider showing more courage on Jeremiah's behalf than any of Judah's own leaders.

verses.text: "those men have been very wicked in all that they have done to the prophet Jeremiah. They have thrown him into a cistern, and he is sure to die of starvation there because there is no food left in the city."

events.title: Zedekiah's Final, Secret Conversation
events.detail: Zedekiah summons Jeremiah once more for a private, sworn-to-secrecy conversation, receiving clear, specific counsel to surrender: advice he privately admits is probably right but is too afraid of his own officials, and of Judean deserters, to actually follow.

verses.text: King Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted to the Babylonians. The Babylonians might hand me over to them, and they will torture me."

eras.label: Era XXXVI · Jeremiah 39
eras.name: The Fall of Jerusalem
eras.dates: After roughly a year and a half under siege, Babylon's army finally breaks through Jerusalem's walls, Zedekiah is captured fleeing and forced to watch his own sons executed before his eyes are put out, and the city and temple are burned to the ground, though Jeremiah himself is specifically protected by Nebuchadnezzar's own direct order.

events.title: The City Falls; Zedekiah's Sons Executed Before His Eyes
events.detail: After the walls are finally breached, Zedekiah is captured fleeing toward Jericho and forced to watch his own sons executed at Riblah before his own eyes are put out and he is led to Babylon in chains, while Nebuchadnezzar issues a direct personal order that Jeremiah, alone among the city's population, is to be protected and treated well.

verses.text: the king of Babylon had Zedekiah's sons put to death while Zedekiah was forced to watch. The king of Babylon also had all the nobles of Judah put to death there. Then he had Zedekiah's eyes put out.
"Find Jeremiah and look out for him. Do not do anything to harm him, but do with him whatever he tells you."

eras.label: Era XXXVII · Jeremiah 40-41
eras.name: Gedaliah's Brief Governorship, and His Assassination
eras.dates: Freed from his chains and given a genuine choice about his own future, Jeremiah stays in the land under the newly appointed governor Gedaliah, whose brief, stabilizing administration is cut violently short when a member of the former royal family assassinates him at a peaceful dinner and massacres dozens of pilgrims besides.

events.title: Jeremiah Set Free, and Gedaliah's Governorship Begins
events.detail: The Babylonian captain personally offers Jeremiah a genuine choice (come to Babylon under royal protection, or remain in the land under the newly appointed governor Gedaliah) and Jeremiah chooses to stay, settling in as Gedaliah begins rebuilding ordinary agricultural life for those left in Judah, despite an early warning of an assassination plot he refuses to believe.

verses.text: "today I will set you free from the chains on your wrists. If you would like to come to Babylon with me, come along and I will take care of you. But if you prefer not to come to Babylon with me, you are not required to do so."

events.title: Gedaliah Assassinated at His Own Dinner Table
events.detail: Ishmael, a member of the former royal family, murders Gedaliah and everyone with him during a shared meal, then slaughters eighty grieving pilgrims and dumps their bodies in an old defensive cistern: an atrocity finally checked when Johanan's forces intercept Ishmael before he can flee to Ammon with the survivors as captives.

verses.text: Ishmael son of Nethaniah and the 10 men who were with him stood up, pulled out their swords, and killed Gedaliah, the son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan.

eras.label: Era XXXVIII · Jeremiah 42-43
eras.name: A Question for the LORD, Disobeyed
eras.dates: Facing an uncertain future after Gedaliah's murder, the remaining Judean leaders solemnly swear to obey whatever answer Jeremiah brings back from the LORD, then flatly disregard it the moment it fails to say what they wanted to hear, forcing Jeremiah himself into exile in Egypt against the LORD's explicit instruction.

events.title: "We Will Obey… Whether We Like It or Not": Until They Don't
events.detail: Johanan and the surviving leaders solemnly ask Jeremiah to seek the LORD's guidance about whether to flee to Egypt, promising in advance to obey "whether we like what he tells us or not": a promise abandoned the instant the answer comes back as a command to stay in the land.

verses.text: "May the LORD [Yahweh] be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not do just as the LORD [Yahweh] your God sends you to tell us to do… whether we like it or not."
"if you people who remain in Judah… say, 'No, we will not stay. Instead we will go and live in the land of Egypt.'"

events.title: Jeremiah Forced Into Egypt Against the LORD's Command
events.detail: Accused of being manipulated by his own scribe Baruch, Jeremiah is forcibly taken to Egypt along with the very people who had sworn to obey him, and once there, he buries stones at Pharaoh's own residence as a sign that Nebuchadnezzar's throne will one day stand on that exact spot.

verses.text: "You are telling a lie! The LORD [Yahweh] our God did not send you to tell us, 'You must not go to Egypt.'… Baruch son of Neriah is stirring you up against us."

eras.label: Era XXXIX · Jeremiah 44
eras.name: The Queen of Heaven, and a Remnant's Refusal to Listen
eras.dates: In Egypt, Jeremiah confronts Judean refugees who openly credit their former prosperity to worshiping the goddess called the Queen of Heaven, and the people, men and women alike, respond with a flat, defiant refusal to stop, becoming the book's final and clearest picture of a remnant that survives judgment only to repeat the very sin that caused it.

events.title: "Why Will You Do Such Great Harm to Yourselves?"
events.detail: Jeremiah confronts the Judean refugee community in Egypt with the visible ruins of Jerusalem as proof of what idolatry brings, asking pointedly why they would repeat the exact behavior that just destroyed their homeland while living as refugees in someone else's country.

events.title: "We Will Not Listen to What You Claim the LORD Has Spoken"
events.detail: In the book's most defiant single response, the refugees (explicitly including the women, who claim their husbands' full approval) announce they will keep worshiping the Queen of Heaven precisely because they remember it as prosperous, becoming the starkest possible illustration that surviving judgment does not automatically produce repentance.

verses.text: "We will not listen to what you claim the LORD [Yahweh] has spoken to us! Instead we will do everything we vowed we would do. We will sacrifice and pour out drink offerings to the goddess called the Queen of Heaven."

eras.label: Era XL · Jeremiah 45
eras.name: A Private Word to Baruch
eras.dates: In the book's shortest chapter, Jeremiah's own scribe Baruch is given a brief, personal message acknowledging his very human exhaustion and grief over the disaster all around him, promised nothing more than his own survival: a small, human-scaled moment tucked between much larger national oracles.

events.title: "I Will Allow You to Escape With Your Life Wherever You Go"
events.detail: In the book's shortest chapter, Baruch's private complaint of exhaustion and hopelessness is met not with grand promises but with a single, modest assurance: his life, and nothing more, will be spared amid the disaster about to fall on everyone else.

verses.text: "Are you looking for great things for yourself? Do not look for such things. For I, the LORD [Yahweh], affirm that I am about to bring disaster on all humanity. But I will allow you to escape with your life wherever you go."

eras.label: Era XLI · Jeremiah 46
eras.name: Oracle Against Egypt
eras.dates: The book's long closing sequence of oracles against foreign nations opens with Egypt, whose army is pictured routed at the historic battle of Carchemish before the prophecy turns to a further, later invasion of Egypt's own homeland by Babylon itself.

events.title: Egypt's Army Routed at Carchemish
events.detail: Egypt's confident army, compared to the rising, turbulent Nile, is pictured shattered at the historic battle of Carchemish, fleeing so completely that "even the swiftest cannot get away" from the LORD's day of reckoning.

verses.text: that day belongs to the Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh] of Heaven's Armies. It is a day of reckoning when he will pay back his adversaries.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar Invades Egypt Itself
events.detail: The oracle looks ahead to a further, direct invasion of Egypt's own territory by Nebuchadnezzar, closing however on the same note of hope extended to Israel throughout the book: disciplined, but never completely destroyed.

verses.text: "I, the LORD [Yahweh], tell you not to be afraid, you descendants of Jacob, my servant, for I am with you… I will indeed discipline you but only in due measure."

eras.label: Era XLII · Jeremiah 47
eras.name: Oracle Against the Philistines
eras.dates: A short but vivid oracle pictures an overwhelming northern flood sweeping away Philistine cities so suddenly that fathers, paralyzed with fear, cannot even turn back to rescue their own children.

events.title: An Overwhelming Flood From the North
events.detail: Philistia's destruction is pictured as a rising flood that overwhelms everything in its path, so terrifying that fleeing fathers are too paralyzed with fear to even turn back and save their own children.

verses.text: Fathers will hear the hoofbeats of the enemies' horses, the clatter of their chariots and the rumbling of their wheels. They will not turn back to save their children because they will be paralyzed with fear.

eras.label: Era XLIII · Jeremiah 48
eras.name: Oracle Against Moab
eras.dates: The book's longest single-nation oracle after Babylon catalogs Moab's coming devastation town by town, mocking its national god Chemosh and its complacent national pride, "like wine allowed to settle undisturbed on its dregs", before closing, like several of these oracles, on an unexpected final note of future restoration.

events.title: "Sure to Be Judged Is Nebo"
events.detail: Town after Moabite town is named for coming destruction, opening a pattern of specific geographic detail that runs through the whole chapter, closing with a curse on anyone who holds back from carrying out the LORD's work of judgment.

events.title: "Like Wine Undisturbed on Its Dregs"
events.detail: Moab's long-unbroken national complacency is compared to wine that has never been poured from jar to jar and so has never had to change: a comfort the chapter promises is about to be violently disrupted, along with Moab's confidence in its national god Chemosh.

verses.text: "Moab has lived undisturbed. It has never been taken into exile. Its people are like wine allowed to settle undisturbed on its dregs, never poured out from one jar to another."

events.title: Weeping for Moab, Despite Everything
events.detail: Even while condemning Moab's arrogance and mockery of Israel, the LORD describes his own heart moaning for Moab "like a flute playing a funeral song": judgment delivered without any hint of satisfaction in the grief it causes.

verses.text: my heart moans for Moab like a flute playing a funeral song. Yes, like a flute playing a funeral song, my heart moans for the people of Kir Heres.

events.title: "Yet in Future Days I Will Reverse Moab's Ill Fortune"
events.detail: Like several of the oracles against the nations, this one closes on an unexpected final note of hope rather than permanent erasure, promising Moab's fortunes will one day be reversed even after total present devastation.

verses.text: "Yet in future days I will reverse Moab's ill fortune," says the LORD [Yahweh]. The judgment against Moab ends here.

eras.label: Era XLIV · Jeremiah 49
eras.name: Oracles Against Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar-Hazor, and Elam
eras.dates: Five shorter oracles move rapidly through Judah's remaining regional neighbors: Ammon accused of illegally occupying Israelite land, Edom warned that even harvest gleaners leave more behind than the LORD intends to, Damascus dissolving into panic, the peaceful desert peoples of Kedar and Hazor caught off guard, and distant Elam promised, like several others, an eventual reversal of fortune.

events.title: Ammon: Land Seized Illegally From Israel
events.detail: Ammon is condemned specifically for occupying territory that belonged to the tribe of Gad after Israel's own exile, with its god Milcom promised exile alongside his priests and officials, though even here, the LORD promises to "reverse Ammon's ill fortune" in days to come.

events.title: Edom: Even Grape Pickers Leave Something Behind
events.detail: Edom's famed wisdom is mocked as having "turned bad," and its confidence in inaccessible mountain hideouts is answered with the chilling promise that even a nest built among the eagles could not put it out of the LORD's reach: worse than an ordinary raid, since even grape pickers and nighttime robbers customarily leave something behind.

verses.text: "If grape pickers came to pick your grapes, would they not leave a few grapes behind?… But I will strip everything away from Esau's descendants."

events.title: Damascus: Courage Melting Into Panic
events.detail: A brief oracle pictures Damascus's famous confidence dissolving instantly into panic and flight, its young soldiers destroyed and its royal palaces set ablaze.

events.title: Kedar and Hazor: Peaceful Peoples Caught Unguarded
events.detail: Unlike fortified cities, the peaceful, undefended desert peoples of Kedar and Hazor are targeted precisely because they have no gates or walls to protect them, their camels and herds carried off as easy plunder.

events.title: Elam: Scattered to the Four Winds
events.detail: The most distant nation in this sequence, Elam, has its military strength (its archers) specifically targeted and its people scattered in every direction, yet closes, like Ammon and Moab before it, with a promise of eventual restored fortune.

verses.text: "Yet in future days I will reverse Elam's ill fortune," says the LORD [Yahweh].

eras.label: Era XLV · Jeremiah 50
eras.name: Babylon Will Fall, and Israel Will Return
eras.dates: The book's longest oracle against a single nation opens with the empire that conquered Jerusalem itself now targeted for the same fate it inflicted on others, its own gods Bel and Marduk put to shame while exiled Israel and Judah are promised a homecoming so complete it amounts to a new, unbreakable covenant.

events.title: "Babylon Will Be Captured. Bel Will Be Put to Shame"
events.detail: The empire that executed judgment on every nation in the preceding chapters is now itself named for destruction, its own gods Bel and Marduk publicly humiliated, while Israel and Judah are promised a genuine, tearful return to seek the LORD together.

verses.text: "Babylon will be captured. Bel will be put to shame. Marduk will be dismayed. Babylon's idols will be put to shame."

events.title: "My People Have Been Lost Sheep"
events.detail: Babylon's earlier gloating over plundering Judah is turned back on itself, while Israel is pictured as sheep gone astray under bad shepherds, promised full forgiveness of guilt once restored to their own good pasture.

verses.text: "I will restore the flock of Israel to their own pasture… no guilt will be found in Israel. No sin will be found in Judah. For I will forgive those of them I have allowed to survive."

events.title: The Hammer That Shattered the Whole World Is Itself Broken
events.detail: Babylon, once described elsewhere as the LORD's own hammer against the nations, is now the one being smashed to pieces, caught like an animal in a trap it never saw laid for it.

verses.text: Babylon hammered the whole world to pieces. But see how that 'hammer' has been broken and shattered!

events.title: A Strong Redeemer Champions Israel's Cause
events.detail: The LORD is described as a powerful redeemer who will "strongly champion" the oppressed cause of Israel and Judah, closing with the same lion-and-shepherd imagery already used against Edom, repurposed almost word for word against Babylon itself.

verses.text: the one who will rescue them is strong. His name is the LORD [Yahweh] of Heaven's Armies. He will strongly champion their cause.

eras.label: Era XLVI · Jeremiah 51
eras.name: "Get Out of Babylon, My People!"
eras.dates: The oracle against Babylon continues at even greater length, moving from a destructive "winnowing wind" and a near-verbatim repetition of the earlier idol-satire hymn through the LORD's own war club imagery, before closing with Jeremiah's associate Seraiah acting out Babylon's permanent sinking with a scroll tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates.

events.title: A Destructive Wind Against Babylon
events.detail: A winnowing wind is summoned specifically against Babylon, urging Judean exiles still living there to flee quickly before judgment arrives "piled up to heaven," while soldiers are told not to spare Babylon's young men or give her archers time to arm themselves.

verses.text: Get out of Babylonia quickly, you foreign people. Flee to save your lives. Do not let yourselves be killed because of her sins, for it is time for the LORD [Yahweh] to wreak his revenge.

events.title: The Idol Satire Repeated Almost Word for Word
events.detail: The hymn to the LORD as maker of heaven and earth, and the mockery of idols as breathless, worthless sham images, returns here nearly verbatim from chapter 10, turning Babylon's own famous idols into exhibit one for the very charge the book has leveled against idolatry throughout.

verses.text: all idolaters will prove to be stupid and ignorant. Every goldsmith will be disgraced by the idol he made. For the image he forges is merely a sham; there is no breath in any of those idols.

events.title: "Babylon, You Are My War Club"
events.detail: In a striking image, Babylon itself is addressed directly as a weapon the LORD once wielded deliberately against other nations: a tool now being discarded and destroyed precisely because it exceeded its purpose and turned to atrocity against Zion.

verses.text: "Babylon, you are my war club, my weapon for battle. I used you to smash nations. I used you to destroy kingdoms."

events.title: "He Will Make Bel Spit Out What He Has Swallowed"
events.detail: Zion's own complaint of having been devoured like prey by Nebuchadnezzar is answered with a promise so vivid it pictures the Babylonian god Bel forced to vomit back up everything he consumed, restoring what was taken.

events.title: "Get Out of Babylon, My People!"
events.detail: A final, urgent evacuation call to any remaining Judean exiles closes the main oracle, promising that heaven and earth alike will one day "sing for joy over Babylon" once the destroyers finally come from the north.

verses.text: "Get out of Babylon, my people! Flee to save your lives from the fierce anger of the LORD [Yahweh]!"

events.title: Seraiah's Scroll, Sunk in the Euphrates
events.detail: Jeremiah sends the entire written oracle against Babylon to Seraiah with instructions for a final, dramatic sign-act: read the scroll aloud once in Babylon itself, then tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates, declaring that Babylon will sink in exactly the same way and never rise again.

verses.text: "When you finish reading this scroll aloud, tie a stone to it and throw it into the middle of the Euphrates River. Then say, 'In the same way Babylon will sink and never rise again.'"

eras.label: Era XLVII · Jeremiah 52
eras.name: Historical Appendix: The Fall of Jerusalem Retold
eras.dates: The book closes not with a prophetic oracle but with a historical appendix, closely paralleling the account in 2 Kings, retelling the siege, the temple's destruction, and the specific numbers of those exiled, before ending on an unexpectedly hopeful final note: the exiled King Jehoiachin, pardoned and elevated decades later in Babylon.

events.title: Zedekiah's Capture Retold
events.detail: The book's final chapter functions as a historical appendix closely paralleling 2 Kings, retelling Zedekiah's failed escape, the execution of his sons before his own eyes, and his blinding and imprisonment in Babylon.

events.title: The Temple Stripped and Burned
events.detail: The Babylonians systematically dismantle and remove Solomon's original temple furnishings (the two famous bronze pillars, the great basin called "The Sea," and every remaining gold and silver vessel) described in enough specific architectural detail to function almost as an inventory of loss.

events.title: Exile Numbered, and Jehoiachin's Unexpected Pardon
events.detail: A precise official count of exiles across three separate deportations closes the historical record, but the book's very last words turn unexpectedly hopeful: decades later, a new Babylonian king releases the long-imprisoned King Jehoiachin, restores him to a position of honor, and gives him a permanent place at the royal table for the rest of his life.

verses.text: King Evil Merodach of Babylon… pardoned King Jehoiachin of Judah and released him from prison. He spoke kindly to him and gave him a more prestigious position than the other kings who were with him in Babylon. Jehoiachin took off his prison clothes and ate daily in the king's presence for the rest of his life.
